analysis.one_liner: Requires the Fed's bank stress tests to add scenarios for rising and falling interest rates.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote and died in the Financial Services Committee when the 118th Congress ended, having drawn no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Banks can fail when interest rates move sharply — in 2023, that is part of what brought down Silicon Valley Bank and forced a government-backed rescue of depositors. The Fed's annual stress tests, which check whether the largest banks have enough capital to survive a crisis, currently must include a baseline and a severely adverse scenario, but the scenarios tested each year are chosen at the Fed's discretion. This bill would have required the Fed's stress tests to always include two additional scenarios: one where interest rates rise sharply and one where they fall. The point is to catch, in advance, banks whose balance sheets would crack under rate swings. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be bank depositors and taxpayers: banks whose capital would fail under a sharp rate move would be identified earlier and forced to build up their buffers before failing, reducing the odds of another taxpayer-backed rescue of uninsured depositors like the one that followed the 2023 bank failures.

how_it_helps.text: The Fed's annual stress tests currently run two mandatory scenarios — baseline and severely adverse. The bill would require five, adding a scenario testing rising interest rates and one testing falling rates [S2][S3].
The bill changes Section 165(i)(1)(B)(i) of the Dodd-Frank-era stress-test provision, striking '2 different' and inserting '5 different' scenarios [S3].
It applies both to bank holding companies and to nonbank financial companies supervised by the Fed, the same category of large firms that were stress-tested after the 2008 crisis [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would fall on large banks and nonbank financial companies, which could be required to hold more capital if they failed the new rate scenarios — a cost they might pass on to borrowers through slightly tighter or costlier credit.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large banks and nonbank financial firms

drawbacks.text: The Federal Reserve already designs its stress-test scenarios each year, and rate movements can appear in its forecasts; hard-coding interest-rate scenarios into statute could reduce the Fed's flexibility to tailor tests to the risks of the moment.
Stricter testing could show that big banks need to hold more capital against rate risk, and banks may pass that cost along through somewhat tighter or costlier lending.

The bill amends only the scenario count and descriptions in one subsection of the Dodd-Frank stress-test provision, so on its own it does not cap bank size, restrict risky activities, or change deposit insurance — it is a narrow diagnostic requirement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is modest but real: banks that survived a 2023-style rate spike without hiding losses would be less likely to fail and hand taxpayers a bailout bill, and depositors' money would be safer. The cost falls on the banks in the form of potentially higher capital requirements, which can be passed along as somewhat costlier credit. The main design question an honest supporter would acknowledge is whether Congress should hard-code interest-rate scenarios into law when the Fed already adjusts its test each year, and whether five mandatory scenarios would sharpen the test or just add compliance weight. On balance it is a targeted fix to a gap exposed in 2023, not a sweeping change.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on June 9, 2023 and referred the same day to the Committee on Financial Services [S1][S5].
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action [S5].
No other House member signed on as a cosponsor over the life of the bill [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired without becoming law [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large banks and nonbank financial firms the bill would have subjected to stricter interest-rate stress testing are better off, because they avoid any chance of being required to hold more capital against rate risk.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large banks facing no added rate testing

for.name: Rep. Brad Sherman
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA), senior member of the House Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; it was referred to the Financial Services Committee, on which he serves.

against.name: Rep. Patrick McHenry
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled it for a hearing or markup; the action history shows nothing after the referral.

sides.party_line_note: Only one member was ever attached to the bill — its Democratic sponsor — so no party bloc ever took a position, and the bill never reached a vote.

industries.industry: Large banks and bank holding companies
industries.note: Adding mandatory rising- and falling-rate scenarios to the Fed's stress tests could reveal thinner capital cushions under rate swings, forcing the biggest banks to hold more capital or shrink risk. That cost falls on bank shareholders and can be passed to borrowers. Interest here runs against the public's stake in bank stability.

industries.industry: Nonbank financial companies supervised by the Fed
industries.note: The bill extends the same added rate scenarios to large nonbank financial firms, closing one of the places where rate risk could hide outside the traditional banking system. These firms' interest in avoiding stricter testing runs against the public's interest in financial stability.
